final_answer:
the 2008 financial crisis began with subprime mortgages—loans given to borrowers with poor credit histories. banks and lenders relaxed lending standards, offering mortgages with low initial rates that later reset to higher levels. as housing prices rose, more people bought homes, creating a housing bubble. 

these risky mortgages were bundled into mortgage-backed securities (mbs), which were sold to investors. to make these securities more attractive, banks created collateralized debt obligations (cdo), which pooled mbs and other debt. investors bought cdo, believing they were safe due to complex rating agencies' high credit ratings. 

banks also used credit default swaps (cdo) to insure against defaults, but this created a web of interconnected risk. excessive leverage—borrowing heavily to invest in these securities—amplified losses when housing prices began to fall. 

when the housing bubble burst in 2007, home prices dropped, leading to defaults. mbs and cdo lost value, and the cdo market collapsed. banks faced massive losses, leading to liquidity crises. major institutions like lehman brothers failed, and others required bailouts. this triggered a global financial meltdown, causing widespread bank failures and a severe recession.
